facts.claim: Searches did not find any published study validating Abbott ARCHITECT hormone immunoassays (total T4, free T4, cortisol, progesterone, insulin) for dog or cat samples. Three targeted searches returned only studies on other platforms (Immulite, Catalyst, enzyme immunoassays) or human-only ARCHITECT evaluations.
facts.source_title: Abbott Architect i2000 Analyzer: An Evaluation of the Reproductive Peptide Hormone Assays (Wheeler & Rossi, 1999) - human only
facts.note: This is a negative finding from a limited search budget, not proof that no study exists. Before launch, ask Abbott India for any veterinary data, or run an in-house validation.

facts.claim: ARCHITECT i2000 chemiluminescent immunoassays use a patented acridinium-derivative tracer. The 1999 evaluation covered human LH, FSH, prolactin and total beta-hCG only.
facts.source_title: Abbott Architect i2000 Analyzer: An Evaluation of the Reproductive Peptide Hormone Assays

facts.topic: 1. ARCHITECT - species-specific assay on the c-module
facts.claim: A canine species-specific immunoturbidimetric CRP assay was validated on the Abbott ARCHITECT c4000 chemistry analyser (Hillstrom et al., 2014) against the Randox canine CRP assay. This shows the ARCHITECT chemistry module can run veterinary species-specific reagents.
facts.source_title: Evaluation of a species-specific C-reactive protein assay for the dog on the ABX Pentra 400 clinical chemistry analyzer
facts.note: This applies to the ARCHITECT c-series, not the i-series immunoassay module.

facts.topic: 1. Human reagents on animal samples - general warning
facts.claim: Using human CRP reagents with heterologous (human) control and calibration material on dog samples can give unpredictable results, including falsely low values.
facts.source_title: Use of heterologous immunoassays for quantification of serum proteins: The case of canine C-reactive protein
facts.note: The search summary quoted this sentence from one of two canine CRP papers (PMC5319752 or PMC5450169). Which of the two it came from is not certain.

facts.topic: 1. Chemiluminescent T4/cortisol in dogs, cats, horses
facts.claim: In a 1997 J Vet Diagn Invest validation of nonradioactive chemiluminescent immunoassays, basal total T4 in dog, cat and horse samples read about 30-40% lower than by RIA and a chemiluminescent-enzyme method. Results were linearly related across methods. Cortisol results were comparable across methods. The methods disagreed on T4 response to T3 suppression in dogs and cats.
facts.source_title: Singh et al. 1997, JVDI: Validation of Nonradioactive Chemiluminescent Immunoassay Methods for T4 and Cortisol in Dogs, Cats, and Horses
facts.note: Not an ARCHITECT assay. It shows that human-calibrated T4 assays can carry a large species bias.

facts.claim: The DPC-Cirrus Immulite automated chemiluminescent cortisol assay was validated for dogs, cats and horses. Dilution behaviour was parallel to the calibration curve, and responses to ACTH stimulation and dexamethasone suppression were as expected.
facts.source_title: Validation and application of solid-phase chemiluminescent immunoassays for diagnosis of endocrine diseases in animals
facts.note: This is the Immulite platform. Use it as a model for an ARCHITECT/MAGLUMI cortisol validation design (parallelism plus ACTH/dex challenge).

facts.claim: Chemiluminescent canine cortisol results should be interpreted with caution unless the specific assay has been adequately validated in dogs.
facts.source_title: Russell et al. 2007, Aust Vet J: Comparison of radioimmunoassay and chemiluminescent assay methods to estimate canine blood cortisol concentrations
facts.note: The search summary called this 'a later review'. Attributing it to Russell 2007 is likely but not verified.

facts.claim: In canine reproduction, mean progesterone by a chemiluminescence assay was significantly higher than by RIA three days before ovulation. Assay choice therefore affects ovulation-timing decisions.
facts.source_title: Comparison of progesterone assay by chemiluminescence or radioimmunoassay for clinical decision-making in canine reproduction
facts.note: The chemiluminescence platform was not named in the snippet. It is not confirmed to be ARCHITECT.

facts.claim: The IDEXX Catalyst Dx progesterone dry-slide immunoassay was validated in canine plasma in a clinical setting against a chemiluminescence assay and mass spectrometry.
facts.source_title: Validation of a dry-slide immunoassay for progesterone analysis in canine plasma in a clinical setting
facts.note: The comparison chemiluminescence platform was not identified in the snippet.

facts.topic: 1. Total T4 assay comparison in dogs and cats
facts.claim: A 2020 JVIM comparison of two serum total T4 assays in dogs found strong correlation (r = 0.99) with proportional bias (slope 0.76) against the reference Microgenics method.
facts.source_title: Wolff et al. 2020, JVIM: Comparison of 2 assays for measuring serum total thyroxine concentration in dogs and cats
facts.note: The snippet did not identify the test assay, so whether it is ARCHITECT is unconfirmed.

facts.claim: A human automated homogeneous T4 enzyme immunoassay was linear from 0-150 nmol/L for human serum, 0-94 nmol/L for feline serum and 10-60 nmol/L for canine serum. The analytical range narrows when a human assay is used on animal serum.
facts.source_title: Horney et al. 1999, Vet Clin Pathol: Evaluation of an Automated, Homogeneous Enzyme Immunoassay for Serum Thyroxine Measurement in Dog and Cat Serum
facts.note: The search summary did not say which of two T4 EIA papers reported these figures (this one or an EIA validation for cats on ResearchGate). Attribution to Horney 1999 is inferred. Not ARCHITECT.

facts.claim: An automated enzyme-linked fluorescent assay was evaluated for T4 measurement in cat and dog sera (Anderson et al., 2017, JVDI).
facts.source_title: Evaluation of an automated enzyme-linked fluorescent assay for thyroxine measurement in cat and dog sera
facts.note: Quantitative findings were not retrieved.

facts.claim: A 2025 study comparing a point-of-care analyser with the IMMULITE 2000 chemiluminescent assay for feline T4 found substantial overall agreement but discordant thyroid-status classification in 15% of samples.
facts.source_title: Evaluation of the analytical performance of a point-of-care analyzer for feline serum thyroxine vs a chemiluminescence enzyme immunoassay

facts.claim: Higgs, Costa, Freke and Papasouliotis (J Small Anim Pract 2014;55:153-159) compared T4 and cortisol measurement in canine and feline samples on two immunoassay analysers. A secondary source reports that mildly to moderately haemolysed or lipaemic samples caused no obvious differences between a fluorescence EIA and the IMMULITE 1000.
facts.source_title: Measurement of thyroxine and cortisol in canine and feline blood samples using two immunoassay analysers
facts.note: Which two analysers were used is unconfirmed. Nothing found ties this paper to ARCHITECT.

facts.claim: Studies compare free T4 by analogue immunoassay against equilibrium dialysis in dogs with non-thyroidal illness, and chemiluminescent immunoassay against tandem mass spectrometry in suspected hypothyroid dogs. Analogue fT4 methods need species-specific checking.
facts.source_title: Free thyroxine measurement by analogue immunoassay and equilibrium dialysis in dogs with non-thyroidal illness
facts.note: Specific numerical findings were not retrieved. A related MS-vs-immunoassay study is at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11899353/

facts.topic: 1. Canine TSH needs a species-specific assay
facts.claim: A commercial canine species-specific TSH immunoassay (Diagnostic Products Corporation) became available in 1997. Several studies have since questioned its diagnostic sensitivity. The TSH stimulation test is accurate in dogs but limited by TSH availability.
facts.source_title: Testing for Hypothyroidism in Dogs (Vet Clin North Am Small Anim Pract)
facts.note: No retrieved source stated directly that human TSH assays fail to detect canine TSH. That specific claim is unconfirmed here.

facts.claim: Canine TSH chemiluminescent immunoassays are commonly used to measure TSH in cats but cannot reliably measure very low concentrations (below 0.03 ng/mL). A newer, more sensitive TSH assay was evaluated for diagnosing feline thyroid disease.
facts.source_title: Evaluation of a novel, sensitive thyroid-stimulating hormone assay as a diagnostic test for thyroid disease in cats

facts.claim: Canine-specific TSH ELISA kits are sold commercially. Abnova KA2296 is labelled research use only (RUO), and ALPCO also lists a Canine TSH ELISA.
facts.source_title: TSH (Canine) ELISA Kit (KA2296) - Abnova
facts.note: ALPCO page: https://www.alpco.com/canine-tsh-elisa.html. These are manual ELISA kits, not ARCHITECT or MAGLUMI reagents. The ALPCO kit's regulatory status was not checked.

facts.claim: In a retrospective study of 301 dogs, DGGR-lipase activity correlated strongly with canine pancreas-specific lipase (Spec cPL). Optimal DGGR cut-offs for predicting cPL >200 and >400 ug/L gave kappa values of 0.87 and 0.92.
facts.source_title: Accuracy of DGGR-Lipase to Predict Canine Pancreas-Specific Lipase (cPL) and Diagnostic Accuracy of Both Tests for Canine Acute Pancreatitis
facts.note: Spec cPL is a species-specific immunoassay (a proprietary IDEXX test, per general knowledge rather than these results). DGGR lipase is a colorimetric substrate assay that can be run on a general chemistry analyser.

facts.topic: 1. Pancreatic lipase - DGGR agreement and cost
facts.claim: Another study reported substantial agreement between DGGR lipase and cPL (kappa 0.679), and noted that DGGR is cheaper and can often be run within an hour at commercial labs.
facts.source_title: PMC5976104 (title not shown in search results)

facts.claim: In dogs recovering from acute pancreatitis, the Roche LIPC DGGR assay and Spec PL gave nearly identical results. Critics note that DGGR is also hydrolysed by hepatic lipase, though the measured effect was minimal.
facts.source_title: Cueni et al. 2023, JVIM: Progression of lipase activity and pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity in dogs hospitalized for acute pancreatitis

facts.claim: Agreement of lipase tests with an ultrasound diagnosis of pancreatitis was weaker (kappa 0.29-0.35).
facts.source_title: Advances in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis in dogs (review)

facts.claim: In a pilot study of 6 dogs with portal hypertension and normal pancreatic histology, Spec cPL exceeded its reference limit more often than DGGR lipase (4/6 vs 2/6).
facts.source_title: Serrano et al. 2021, JVDI: Increased cPLI and DGGR lipase in dogs with portal hypertension and normal pancreatic histology

facts.claim: In dogs with chronic kidney disease, SNAP cPL was abnormal more often than DGGR lipase. The authors suggested SNAP cPL may overestimate pancreatic involvement.
facts.source_title: Assessment of Pancreatic Lipase Activity Using a Quantitative and a Qualitative Assay in Dogs with Chronic Kidney Disease

facts.claim: No official Snibe veterinary reagent line or veterinary MAGLUMI analyser was found. Snibe's own site lists MAGLUMI analysers (X3, X6, X8, X10, 800, 600, 2000, 2000 Plus) under clinical (human) CLIA diagnostics. The MAGLUMI X3 page cites a test menu of up to 278 parameters.
facts.source_title: MAGLUMI X3 - Snibe Diagnostic
facts.note: Absence of a vet line is a negative search finding. Confirm with Snibe India.

facts.claim: Some online marketplace sellers list a 'MAGLUMI 800 ... Veterinary Instrument' at USD 3,900-7,000, with no canine or feline assay menu.
facts.source_title: Alibaba listing - Snibe Maglumi 800
facts.note: Unverified reseller marketing, not Snibe documentation. Do not rely on it.

facts.claim: No peer-reviewed study validating any MAGLUMI assay (T4, cortisol, progesterone or other) in dogs, cats or cattle was found. The available chemiluminescence validation literature in animals concerns Immulite and other platforms.
facts.source_title: Validation and application of solid-phase chemiluminescent immunoassays for diagnosis of endocrine diseases in animals (Immulite)
facts.note: Negative search result. An in-house validation would be required.

facts.claim: Samples from animals with nucleated erythrocytes and thrombocytes (birds, reptiles, amphibians) cannot be analysed by an automated haematology analyser at the Michigan State University VDL. Manual methods are needed.
facts.source_title: MSU VDL - Hematology & Hemostasis
facts.note: Directly relevant to poultry: avian CBC needs manual counts and smear review.

facts.claim: Platelet clumping can falsely decrease the platelet count and increase MPV. A reported automated count in that situation should be treated as a minimum.
facts.source_title: MSU VDL - Hematology & Hemostasis

facts.claim: Most automated haematology analysers cannot perform platelet counts in cats because feline platelet and erythrocyte sizes overlap. Feline platelet numbers generally must be estimated from a stained blood film or counted manually.
facts.source_title: Harvey 2017, J Feline Med Surg: The feline blood film: 1. Techniques and erythrocyte morphology

facts.topic: 3. Hematology limits - reporting practice at a reference lab
facts.claim: Cornell AHDC flags platelet clumps and reports a platelet count only when its (veterinary-configured) Advia analyser gives a relatively accurate count. Its total leukocyte and absolute differential counts are not corrected for nucleated RBCs, which the analyser does not quantify individually, so smear review is required.
facts.source_title: Cornell AHDC - Hematology testing protocols

facts.claim: A US patent states that conventional counting methods are not suitable for a CBC in birds, reptiles and fish (nucleated RBCs and thrombocytes) or in certain mammals whose RBCs are very small and may be confused with platelets.
facts.source_title: US patent: Method and apparatus for determining red blood cell indices ... intrinsic pigmentation of hemoglobin
facts.note: Patent text, not peer-reviewed. Goat or sheep microcytic RBC data were not retrieved.

facts.claim: ASVCP has published quality assurance guidelines for preanalytical and analytical factors in haematology for mammalian and non-mammalian species, hemostasis and crossmatching (Vap et al., 2012, Vet Clin Pathol).
facts.source_title: ASVCP QA guidelines: hematology for mammalian and nonmammalian species, hemostasis, crossmatching (Vap 2012)

facts.claim: Mindray's veterinary products are sold by a separate entity, Shenzhen Mindray Animal Medical Technology Co., Ltd., which markets the BC-60R Vet as an automatic benchtop 6-part-differential veterinary haematology analyser.
facts.source_title: MedicalExpo - BC-60R Vet - Shenzhen Mindray Animal Medical Technology

facts.claim: BC-60R Vet: 6-part leukocyte differential, 33 haematology parameters, SF-Cube 3D (scatter plus fluorescence) technology that flags bands and nucleated RBCs, about 40 samples/hour, storage for up to 40,000 results.
facts.source_title: Mindray BC-60R Vet - Medexpert (distributor)
facts.note: Distributor data. Sample volume is quoted as 31 or 34 uL by different sources (unconfirmed). Manufacturer brochure: https://equiposmedicosveterinariosmb.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Mindray-BC-60R-Vet-brochure.pdf

facts.claim: Mindray Animal's BC-60R Vet page describes a 'special friendly for feline' design and broad species coverage including rabbits, birds, fishes, reptiles, amphibians, alpacas and pigs. One distributor lists 16 species: cat, dog, horse, rat, mouse, rabbit, monkey, pig, cow, ferret, goat, sheep, camel, llama, panda, alpaca.
facts.source_title: BC-60R Vet - Mindray Animal
facts.note: Buffalo is not listed in any source, and whether avian CBC is fully automated is unclear. Verify the current species list with Mindray India.

facts.topic: 3. Mindray BC-60R Vet - phased species rollout
facts.claim: A Chinese supplier listing describes BC-60R Vet species software released in phases: Phase I cat, dog, horse; Phase II rodents, rabbit, monkey, pig, camel, llama; Phase III cow, ferret, goat, sheep, panda, alpaca.
facts.source_title: Made-in-China listing - Mindray BC-60R Vet
facts.note: Reseller listing, about 2.5 years old. Phase status may be outdated.

facts.claim: BC-5000 Vet (5-part differential veterinary analyser) is reported with 13 built-in species (dog, cat, horse, monkey, ferret, rat, mouse, rabbit, pig, cow, llama, goat, sheep) plus 20 user-programmable animal profiles.
facts.source_title: BC-5000 Vet - Elokarsa (distributor)
facts.note: Distributor data. An older ~2014 datasheet (https://5.imimg.com/data5/SELLER/Doc/2022/6/PF/NI/MI/26356964/mindray-bc-5000vet-veterinary-hematology-analyzer.pdf) showed several species as 'coming' in Sept/Dec 2014.

facts.claim: No Mindray or distributor page for a 'BC-6000 Vet' was found. Whether that model exists is unconfirmed. No source was found on adding a veterinary species mode to the lab's human BC-6800/BC-6000/BC-760 series.
facts.source_title: BC-60R Vet - Mindray Animal (search context)
facts.note: Negative finding. Ask Mindray whether the existing human 7-part analyser can be licensed with veterinary software. Otherwise a dedicated vet analyser would be needed.

facts.claim: BioSystems S.A. markets the BA200 for veterinary analysis. Its 2025 veterinary brochure says that, with original BA reagents validated for veterinary analysis (a veterinary panel including special biochemistry tests), the BA200 forms a complete system.
facts.source_title: BioSystems 2025 VET Brochure - BA200
facts.note: Manufacturer claim. No independent peer-reviewed validation of the BA200 on animal samples was found.

facts.claim: The BA200 has 88 reagent/sample positions and an optional ISE module with sodium, potassium, chloride and reference electrodes.
facts.source_title: BioSystems 2025 VET Brochure - BA200

facts.claim: BioSystems' veterinary reagent pages offer biochemistry reagents for more than 120 parameters. The reagent selector filters by species category (Canine, Feline, Bovine, Camels, Equine, Poultry, Reptiles/Exotic) and by analyser (A15, A25, BA200, BA400).
facts.source_title: BioSystems - Veterinary reagents
facts.note: There is no buffalo or goat category in the snippet. Which assays are claimed for which species was not retrieved.

facts.claim: The BioSystems veterinary product list includes BA200/BA400 reagent codes, for example ALT/GPT (11568, 11562) and albumin (21547, 23547).
facts.source_title: BioSystems 2022 Veterinary Product List
facts.note: The codes come from a search snippet. Verify them against the current list before ordering.

facts.claim: BioSystems has a dedicated 'VetBC reference materials' page under its veterinary biochemistry systems, indicating veterinary calibrator/control materials.
facts.source_title: BioSystems - VetBC reference materials
facts.note: The page exists but its contents (matrix, analytes, species) were not retrieved.

facts.topic: 4. Albumin by BCG - heparin plasma in dogs
facts.claim: In clinically ill dogs, BCG albumin was higher in heparinised plasma than in serum or citrated plasma, mainly because of fibrinogen. The authors advised against heparin for BCG albumin unless the assay uses a sample blank and a reaction time under 1 minute.
facts.source_title: Stokol et al. 2001, Vet Clin Pathol: Overestimation of canine albumin with the BCG method in heparinized plasma

facts.claim: Compared with electrophoresis, BCG albumin was on average higher in horse and dog samples, and in cat samples when BCG was 2.5 g/dL or less. The bias reversed (BCG lower) in chickens and ruminants.
facts.source_title: Comparison of Electrophoretic and Bromocresol Green Albumin Methods in Chickens and Other Veterinary Species (2025)

facts.topic: 4. Albumin - BCG vs BCP in animals
facts.claim: BCG is used in veterinary medicine because BCP has lower affinity for animal albumin, though BCG slightly overestimates. BCG-BCP agreement was good only for horse sera.
facts.source_title: Acta Vet Brno 2020: Serum albumin assay (review)
facts.note: An older study also found BCP gave significantly lower values in dog and rat plasma: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/002199758890093X . Human BCP albumin reagents should not be used for dogs or cats without validation.

facts.claim: Acute-phase globulins contribute to BCG albumin overestimation. BCG and BCP results can differ enough to cause clinical confusion, especially at low albumin concentrations.
facts.source_title: Lab Medicine: Overestimation of Albumin Measured by BCG vs BCP: Influence of Acute-Phase Globulins
facts.note: Species studied not clear from the snippet. Possibly human.

facts.claim: No sources were retrieved on species-specific performance of enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, CK), fructosamine, bile acids or electrolytes on the BA200 or other human chemistry analysers.
facts.source_title: Analytical performance and method comparison of a POC immunoassay for bile acids in cats and dogs (only tangential result found)
facts.note: Gap. Needs further searching.

facts.topic: 5. ASVCP QA - method validation before use
facts.claim: ASVCP guidelines say method or instrument validation should be done before a new test or instrument is adopted, to confirm it meets the lab's standards and the manufacturer's claims. Validation may assess linearity, precision, accuracy, analytical range, detection limits and interfering substances. Reference intervals and QC procedures should be set before patient testing. Participation in a veterinary-specific external proficiency testing programme is recommended.
facts.source_title: Flatland et al. 2010, Vet Clin Pathol 39:264-277: ASVCP QA guidelines - control of general analytical factors in veterinary laboratories

facts.claim: ASVCP Guidelines: Principles of Quality Assurance and Standards for Veterinary Clinical Pathology, version 3.0 (Arnold et al., 2019, Vet Clin Pathol), is the current consolidated QALS guideline.
facts.source_title: Arnold et al. 2019: ASVCP Guidelines v3.0
facts.note: Full text PDF (233 pages): https://repository.up.ac.za/bitstream/handle/2263/76138/Arnold_ASVCP_2019.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y

facts.claim: ASVCP also published QA guidelines for preanalytical, analytical and postanalytical factors in urinalysis, cytology and clinical chemistry (Gunn-Christie et al., 2012, Vet Clin Pathol).
facts.source_title: Gunn-Christie et al. 2012: ASVCP QA guidelines for urinalysis, cytology, clinical chemistry

facts.claim: ASVCP has guidelines on external quality assessment and comparative testing for reference and in-clinic laboratories (Camus et al., 2015, Vet Clin Pathol).
facts.source_title: Camus et al. 2015: ASVCP QA guidelines - external quality assessment and comparative testing

facts.claim: The ASVCP allowable total error (TEa) guidelines for biochemistry (Harr, Flatland, Nabity, Freeman; Vet Clin Pathol 2013;42(4):424-436) recommend TEa values for common biochemical analytes in cats, dogs and horses. They apply to all veterinary settings, from in-clinic POC to reference labs. An erratum was published in Vet Clin Pathol 2018;47(1):170.
facts.source_title: Harr et al. 2013: ASVCP guidelines - allowable total error guidelines for biochemistry
facts.note: The actual TEa table values were not retrieved. PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24320779/

facts.claim: ASVCP has also published allowable total error guidelines for haematology.
facts.source_title: ASVCP guidelines: Allowable total error hematology
facts.note: Year, authors and values were not retrieved.

facts.claim: ASVCP published point-of-care testing QA guidelines (Flatland et al., 2013, Vet Clin Pathol 42:405-423).
facts.source_title: QALS Guidelines - Veterinary Clinical Pathology (Wiley)

facts.claim: The ASVCP reference interval guidelines (Friedrichs et al., 2012, Vet Clin Pathol 41(4):441-453) recommend at least 120 reference individuals for nonparametric limits with 90% confidence intervals, plus extra animals to allow outlier removal. With fewer than 120, bootstrapping or similar methods are needed for the 90% CIs. 39 is the smallest number from which a nonparametric 95% interval can be obtained, with the extreme values serving as the limits.
facts.source_title: Friedrichs et al. 2012: ASVCP reference interval guidelines - de novo reference intervals in veterinary species
facts.note: Table 4 of the guideline gives method choice by sample size. It was not retrieved.

facts.claim: ASVCP RI guidance states that reference intervals should not be determined when fewer than 20 reference samples are available.
facts.source_title: ASVCP QALS - RI Guidelines (website version)
facts.note: Taken from a search summary. A secondary blog phrased it as 'between 10 and 20 samples the RI should not be determined' (https://medium.com/@tentotheminus9/veterinary-stats-reference-intervals-765ac7656d1). The exact thresholds (n<10 vs 10-19 vs 20-39) need checking in the primary text.

facts.claim: Per a citing paper, the ASVCP guidelines do not recommend partitioning reference intervals by age or sex when sample sizes are below 40.
facts.source_title: ASVCP reference interval guidelines (ResearchGate)
facts.note: Secondary citation. Verify in the primary guideline.

facts.claim: Secondary sources report that ASVCP guidance supports the robust method (with bootstrapped CIs) for intermediate sample sizes, e.g. one paper used it for 100-120 individuals.
facts.source_title: Veterinary Stats - Reference Intervals (blog)
facts.note: Secondary sources only. Exact sample-size ranges are unconfirmed.

facts.claim: The ASVCP Reference Interval Transference verification checklist calls for samples from 20 reference individuals from the laboratory's own healthy patient population. Verification confirms that using the candidate RI is acceptable and will not cause clinical error.
facts.source_title: ASVCP - Reference Interval Transference: Verification Checklist and Flow Chart v.1

facts.claim: CLSI EP28-A3c recommends analysing a minimum of 20 samples from healthy individuals to verify a reference interval.
facts.source_title: Verification of reference intervals in routine clinical laboratories: practical challenges and recommendations

facts.claim: Transferred limits are verified with a binomial test of the proportion of 20 observations inside the interval against an expected 0.95. A worked example with 18/20 inside (0.90) gave exact p = 0.2642, so the interval was not rejected. This is consistent with the commonly used 'no more than 2 of 20 outside' rule.
facts.source_title: Analyse-it - EP28-A3C reference interval example
facts.note: No retrieved source states the '<=2 of 20 outside' rule verbatim. Check the CLSI document (preview: https://webstore.ansi.org/preview-pages/CLSI/preview_CLSI+C28-A3.pdf).

facts.claim: A summary of EP28-A3c lists three ways to verify transferred intervals: subjective assessment, a small sample of about 20, and larger samples of up to 60. It notes that 20 samples may lack statistical power.
facts.source_title: CLSI EP28-A3c: Verifying Reference Intervals (Scribd copy)
facts.note: Secondary summary, not the standard itself.

facts.claim: No sources on CLSI EP15 (precision and trueness verification) or EP09 (method comparison) in a veterinary context were retrieved.
facts.source_title: ASVCP Guidelines v3.0 (likely to reference them)
facts.note: Gap. The search budget was exhausted.

research.gaps:
I used all 18 searches, so these points are still open:

1. **ARCHITECT:** I found no published dog or cat validation of any ARCHITECT immunoassay (T4, free T4, cortisol, progesterone, insulin). I could not tell which platforms the Wolff 2020 and Higgs 2014 comparisons used. Nothing was found on insulin cross-reactivity between species.
2. **Snibe MAGLUMI:** I found no official Snibe veterinary reagent line and no peer-reviewed MAGLUMI validation in any animal species. The only "veterinary" claims are on reseller listings.
3. **Mindray:**
   - I found no source on running animal blood on the lab's human 7-part analyser (BC-6800, BC-6000 or BC-760), or on licensing veterinary species software for it.
   - I could not confirm that a "BC-6000 Vet" exists.
   - Mindray's own current species list for the BC-60R Vet was not retrieved; distributor lists disagree.
   - No source covered buffalo, and nothing gave goat or sheep microcytic red-cell data.
4. **BioSystems BA200:**
   - I found no independent validation in animals.
   - I found no species-specific data for enzymes, lipase, fructosamine, bile acids or electrolytes.
   - The VetBC reference materials page exists, but I could not read what it contains.
   - I did not cover veterinary third-party control materials or the human-matrix calibrator problem in general.
5. **ASVCP and CLSI:**
   - I did not retrieve the actual TEa values (Harr 2013, and the haematology TEa guideline).
   - I did not retrieve Friedrichs 2012 Table 4 (method choice by sample size); the thresholds for groups of 10–20 and 20–39 animals need checking against the primary text.
   - No source stated the "no more than 2 of 20 outside" rule word for word.
   - CLSI EP15 and EP09 were not searched.
6. **India:** I found no Indian government, regulator or NABL source on accrediting veterinary labs or on rules for veterinary IVD reagents.
7. **Pancreatic lipase:** I found nothing on feline pancreatic lipase (fPL) or on whether ARCHITECT or MAGLUMI can run species-specific pancreatic lipase immunoassays. The DGGR lipase studies are dog only.

checks.claim: A canine species-specific immunoturbidimetric CRP assay was validated on the Abbott ARCHITECT c4000 (Hillstrom et al., 2014) against the Randox canine CRP assay (cited URL: PMC5450169).
checks.reason: The validation on the ARCHITECT c4000 is confirmed. The assay was Gentian cCRP, calibrated with canine CRP from Life Diagnostics. Two details are wrong. First, the comparator was a Randox human CRP assay previously validated for dogs, not a Randox canine assay. Second, PMC5450169 is a different paper (canine CRP on the ABX Pentra 400). The correct citation is Hillstrom, Hagman, Tvedten and Kjelgaard-Hansen, Vet Clin Pathol 2014;43(2):235-243. Its limit of quantification was 6.8 mg/L, and healthy dogs fell below it. A follow-up study reported that quality criteria were met on the ARCHITECT c4000 and the Olympus AU600. This applies to the c-series chemistry module only, not to i-series immunoassays.
checks.corrected_value: Gentian cCRP on ARCHITECT c4000, compared with a Randox human CRP assay previously validated for dogs; source DOI 10.1111/vcp.12150

checks.claim: Wolff et al. 2020 JVIM: comparing two total T4 assays in dogs gave r = 0.99 with proportional bias (slope 0.76) against the Microgenics reference method; the test assay is unidentified.
checks.reason: The two assays tested against Microgenics DRI TT4 (MTT4) were IDEXX Catalyst TT4 (CTT4) and Siemens Immulite 2000 TT4 (ITT4). The slope of 0.76 belongs to the Immulite 2000 in dogs; in cats it was 0.71, and the authors say ITT4 underestimates TT4. For Catalyst versus MTT4 in dogs, the slope was 0.86 (95% CI 0.83-0.89) with a constant bias of 0.10 ug/dL. In cats, Catalyst had slope 1.01 but failed the linearity test. The r = 0.99 figure was not found. Neither assay is ARCHITECT or MAGLUMI. The authors advise doing serial TT4 measurements on the same assay. A 2025 letter (PMC11984318) disputes the paper's conclusion for cats.
checks.corrected_value: Immulite 2000 vs MTT4: slope 0.76 (dogs), 0.71 (cats); Catalyst vs MTT4 (dogs): slope 0.86, intercept 0.10 ug/dL; r = 0.99 unconfirmed

checks.claim: In a retrospective study of 301 dogs, DGGR-lipase correlated strongly with Spec cPL; optimal DGGR cut-offs for cPL >200 and >400 ug/L gave kappa values of 0.87 and 0.92.

A DGGR cut-off of 143 U/L predicted cPL >200 ug/L (Se 91.7%, Sp 95.3%, kappa 0.87). A cut-off of 205 U/L predicted cPL >=400 ug/L (Se 97.5%, Sp 96.4%, kappa 0.92). For clinical AP, the AUCs were 0.75 for DGGR and 0.76 for cPL. Note that the second threshold is >=400, not >400. Cut-offs depend on the method and population: Hope et al. 2021 JSAP reported >42.15 U/L on a different DGGR method. A lab adopting DGGR on the BA200 must therefore set its own cut-off.

Sensitivity, specificity and PPV for hyperthyroidism were about 90.5%, 98.9% and 86.9% for BAW, versus 79.9%, 76.7% and 21.7% for chemiluminescence. A 2026 JFMS follow-up found BAW more specific. The ASVCP QALS website version states that RIs should not be determined with fewer than 20 reference samples. For 20 to under 40 samples, it recommends parametric methods (if Gaussian, with 90% CIs) or robust methods. It recommends at least 120 samples for nonparametric limits with 90% CIs. The use of bootstrapped CIs for fewer than 120 samples matches the guideline text already cited. The exact Table 4 wording for 40-119 was not fully retrieved. A 2019 simulation study (Le Boedec, Vet Clin Pathol) suggests nonparametric methods may sometimes be preferable even for small samples.

checks.claim: CLSI EP28-A3c transference verification: a binomial test with 18/20 inside gave exact p = 0.2642, so the interval was not rejected; this is consistent with the 'no more than 2 of 20 outside' rule.
checks.reason: The arithmetic is correct: under coverage 0.95, P(X <= 18 of 20) = 0.2642. But the binomial test is less strict than the '<=2 of 20 outside' rule, so the two are not equivalent. With 3 of 20 outside, P(X <= 17) = 0.0755, which is still above 0.05, so a one-sided binomial test at alpha 0.05 would not reject an interval that the 2-of-20 rule would reject. These probabilities are my own calculation, not from a search source. The verbatim '<=2 of 20' rule is still not confirmed from the CLSI text in any retrieved source. The ASVCP transference checklist (20 animals) is the veterinary-specific reference.

Note that the 'USD 430.0 million by 2033 at 7% CAGR' figure the researcher attributed to openpr is IMARC's own earlier edition (USD 230.0 M in 2024), not an independent estimate. Other firms: MarketsandMarkets USD 111.5 M (2025) to USD 181.3 M (2030) at 10.2%; GII listing USD 224.61 M (FY2024) to USD 460.11 M (FY2032) at 9.38%. Present this as a range, not a single number.

checks.claim: IMARC: India pet care products market USD 8.6 billion (2025) to USD 13.9 billion by 2034, 5.24% CAGR.
checks.reason: The IMARC page shows these figures. The same search shows that IMARC's figures are internally inconsistent (another IMARC page cites USD 23.84 bn for 2025). Other estimates for 2025 range from USD 628 M (Research and Markets) and USD 777 M (Expert Market Research) to USD 4.3 bn (Ken Research) and USD 14.8 bn (Fortune Business Insights). Redseer gives USD 3.6 bn total pet spend in 2024 and at least USD 7 bn by 2028. Scope varies, so do not present any one figure as the market size.

checks.claim: Expert Market Research: India pet care products market USD 777.02 million in 2025, 23.70% CAGR to 2035.
checks.reason: The figure and CAGR appear in the re-search results. It is a narrow products-only scope, so it is not comparable with IMARC's USD 8.6 bn.

checks.claim: IMARC: India pet food market USD 2.52 billion in 2025.
checks.reason: Re-search returned the same 2025 figure. The 2026 estimate, 2034 projection and 6.91% CAGR were not separately re-checked.

checks.claim: Euromonitor: India's pet population grew about 5% in 2024, with similar growth expected in 2025, reaching 39 million pets.
checks.reason: Confirmed from the Euromonitor report page. 39 million is the expected 2025 level, not a 2024 count. Conflicting secondary figures: one industry article citing Euromonitor says 42 million in 2024 (up from 26 million in 2019), and Ken Research says about 42.2 million companion pets in 2024. Label 39 million as a Euromonitor 2025 projection.

checks.claim: Indian survey of 525 dogs: Hepatozoon canis was the most common tick-borne pathogen (30%), followed by Ehrlichia canis (20.6%). 39% of infected dogs had more than one pathogen, and PCR was more sensitive than blood-smear examination.
checks.reason: Megat Abd Rani et al., Parasites & Vectors 4:141 (2011), four Indian cities. Further detail: PCR found at least one pathogen in 49.7% of dogs, while smears found Hepatozoon in only 2.3%. Other PCR prevalences were Mycoplasma haemocanis 12.2%, Anaplasma platys 6.5%, Babesia vogeli 5.5% and B. gibsoni 0.2%. Ticks were found on 53% of dogs. The data are from 2011, so describe them as such.

checks.claim: NDDB and the Government of Maharashtra signed an MoU in 2013 for dairy development in Vidarbha and Marathwada (VMDDP), with Mother Dairy (an NDDB subsidiary) providing market access. Sources disagree on the number of districts (7, 10 or 11).
checks.reason: The 2013 MoU and Mother Dairy's role are confirmed. On districts: re-search found the project running in 10 districts since 2016: Akola, Amravati, Wardha, Nagpur, Chandrapur and Buldhana in Vidarbha, and Nanded, Osmanabad, Latur and Jalna in Marathwada. Nagpur district is included. A 2024 News On AIR report says the scheme had covered 11 districts before Phase 2. Procurement began in October 2016 with 175 kg of milk from 12 villages on day one. One source says the project later covered 3,411 villages and about 35,000 farmers.

checks.claim: VMDDP procurement later averaged 1,85,000 litres a day from 1,454 milk pooling points.
checks.reason: No re-search result showed these figures. More recent figures found: about 4 lakh litres a day from about 35,000 farmers through 2,500 milk pooling points (early 2025, Marathvarhad MPO coverage). The 1.85 lakh L/day figure is probably outdated.

checks.claim: Marathvarhad MPO: women-owned, incorporated 9 Jan 2025 with its registered office in Nagpur. Collected about 4 lakh L/day from about 35,000 farmers. Targets 6,000 villages, 1.85 lakh women members and 11 lakh kg/day within 5 years.
checks.reason: All figures are confirmed by FFOODS Spectrum and AgriMoon/Indian Cooperative (early 2025), plus 2,500 milk pooling points and direct bank payments to members. No 2026 update on membership or volumes was found. A Free Press Journal piece reports women from 6 districts trading nearly 3.75 lakh litres a day (date not confirmed). Describe these as early-2025 figures.

checks.claim: In November 2023 Nitin Gadkari laid the foundation stone for Mother Dairy's greenfield plant on 25 acres at Butibori, Nagpur, with 6 lakh L/day capacity expandable to 10 lakh.
checks.reason: Confirmed by Mother Dairy's 24 Nov 2023 press release and trade coverage, including an investment of more than Rs 500 crore and a product mix of pouch milk, ice cream, chaach, lassi and paneer. No report of commissioning or inauguration was found. Operating status as of Oct 2026 is unconfirmed, so call it 'under development' unless verified.

checks.claim: In August 2024 Maharashtra approved more than Rs 149 crore for Phase 2 of the dairy development programme covering all 19 districts of Vidarbha and Marathwada.
checks.reason: Cabinet decision reported 13 Aug 2024. Before Phase 2 the scheme covered 11 districts. One report gives a total project cost of Rs 328.42 crore, with Rs 179.16 crore from farmers and livestock owners; how this relates to the Rs 149 crore is unclear. No later rollout status was found.

facts.topic: 4. Sample handling - serum and EDTA shipping
facts.claim: Purdue's guidelines say to let blood clot 15-30 min, centrifuge 10 min, transfer the serum to an additive-free tube, and ship overnight on an ice pack, avoiding heat and freezing. Smears from samples older than about 8 h may be inadequate, and tube and slides should not touch the ice pack directly.

research.gaps:
I used 17 of the 18 shared WebSearch calls. These items were not confirmed and need follow-up:
(a) Indian prevalence or demand data for canine distemper, and Indian PCR prevalence for FeLV, FIV and FCoV. Only feline panleukopenia (FPV) has Indian data.
(b) Whether Spec cPL is proprietary to IDEXX was not sourced. SDMA's IDEXX patent was confirmed.
(c) No source was found for T4, cortisol/ACTH stimulation/LDDST, fructosamine, bile acids or UPC test-menu specifics, or for veterinary validation of human immunoassays for these analytes.
(d) Nothing came back on the NADCP brucellosis programme, bovine metabolic profiles (Ca, BHB), Mycoplasma gallisepticum testing labs in India, Newcastle disease/IBD RT-PCR kits, or small-ruminant panels beyond brucellosis and Johne's disease.
(e) No Indian-made commercial veterinary qPCR kit for canine tick-borne pathogens, CPV or CDV was found. Searches on TRUPCR/3B BlackBio, Genes2Me, Huwel and Imgenex returned nothing veterinary. Only Retro Biotech (Jaipur) appeared, with a Brucella-containing multiplex.
(f) Bio-Rad CFX96 and Qiagen Rotor-Gene compatibility was not confirmed for any veterinary kit. Thermo VetMAX kits are confirmed only on ABI 7500/7500 Fast and QuantStudio 5.
(g) No Vidarbha- or Nagpur-specific prevalence studies turned up.
(h) No sources were found for PCR swab transport media and stability, ACTH pre-analytical stability details, or published turnaround-time standards. The only turnaround benchmarks are the Vetic same-day claim and DGGR lipase reported within about 1 h.
Several entries are marked confirmed=false because the search summary did not make clear which URL carried the figure.

checks.claim: A survey of 525 dogs in four Indian cities found 261 dogs infected with at least one tick-borne pathogen by PCR. H. canis 30%, E. canis 20.6%, A. platys 6.5%, B. gibsoni 0.2% (Abd Rani et al., Parasites & Vectors 2011).
checks.reason: Search results confirm 261/525 (49.7%) PCR-positive, H. canis 30%, E. canis 20.6%, A. platys 6.5% and B. gibsoni 0.2%. The researcher left out two figures: Mycoplasma haemocanis 12.2% and B. vogeli 5.5%. Co-infection was 39%. Smear microscopy found Hepatozoon in only 12/525 (2.3%), which supports PCR over smear. The data are about 15 years old.

checks.claim: PCR study of 130 dogs in Mizoram and Tripura: about half infected; B. gibsoni 43% (most common), H. canis 38%; Mizoram 58% vs Tripura 44% (Parasites & Vectors 2019).
checks.reason: Overall 68/130 (52%) positive. B. gibsoni 56/130 (43%), H. canis 50/130 (38%), Mizoram 58% vs Tripura 44%. Other findings: co-infection in 34%, A. platys 3%, B. vogeli 3%, A. reconditum 2%, D. immitis 2%.

checks.claim: Gujarat study (Veterinary World, July 2026) of 100 dogs and 100 cats: 85% of dogs CPV-positive; quantitative PCR detected 62% of infections vs 19.5% for conventional PCR.
checks.reason: The 62.0% (qPCR) and 19.5% (conventional VP2 PCR) figures are positivity rates across all 200 faecal samples, dogs and cats together. They are not shares of infections, and they are not dog-only figures. Duplex probe qPCR found 85 CPV-positive dogs out of 100, so 85% is right for qPCR. Rapid antigen tests flagged 40.0% as CPV-positive and 5.0% as FPV-positive. CPV was found in 12% of cats and FPV in 1% of dogs. Samples were collected from September 2024 to September 2025. Also indexed as PMC13500128 / PMID 42634831.
checks.corrected_value: Across 200 samples (100 dogs + 100 cats): duplex qPCR 62.0% positive vs conventional PCR 19.5% vs rapid antigen test 40% (CPV) / 5% (FPV); 85/100 dogs CPV-positive by qPCR; CPV in 12% of cats

checks.claim: The DLD SDMA ELISA (designed for human samples) showed much larger bias against LC-MS than the IDEXX SDMA Test (PLOS ONE 2018).
checks.reason: Ernst et al. 2018 tested 30 pooled canine and 30 pooled feline sera. Over 10-45 ug/dL, estimated bias was about 1-2 ug/dL for IDEXX and 5-8 ug/dL for DLD. At low concentrations, CV was 7.7% for IDEXX and 31.1% for DLD. The paper's regression slopes are inconsistent between abstract and results, so do not quote slopes. A 2024 JVIM study in older dogs also found ELISA SDMA higher than LC-MS/MS (mean difference about 2.2 ug/dL) and recommended assay-specific reference intervals.

checks.claim: IDEXX Laboratories holds a patent on the ELISA methodology for measuring SDMA.
checks.reason: The search on the PLOS ONE paper did not bring up the patent. A second search did list USPTO patents titled 'Antibodies to symmetrically dimethylated arginine analytes and use thereof' (US 11384158 and US 11136412), but the results did not show who holds them or what they claim. Do not state 'IDEXX patent' as fact in the deck. Say the validated SDMA immunoassay is an IDEXX product.

checks.claim: A 2025 study evaluated the IDEXX SDMA immunoassay on a Beckman Coulter analyser using IDEXX reagent kits and described it as the first fully automated SDMA immunoassay.
checks.reason: Kodger et al., Clin Chim Acta vol 579 (January 2026, online 30 Sep 2025), is a human clinical-chemistry study. Its reference intervals come from human samples in the ADLM (formerly AACC) sample bank, and it compares the assay with LC-MS/MS. A related 2025 Clinical Chemistry abstract names the analyser as the Beckman Coulter AU5800. The study says nothing about veterinary use or about IDEXX reagents being sold to third-party labs in India, so it cannot be used to argue that the BA200 or any Dhruv analyser could run veterinary SDMA. Sample counts differ between sources (over 500 vs 611).
checks.corrected_value: Human-sample study (ADLM sample bank) of the automated IDEXX SDMA immunoassay on a Beckman Coulter AU5800, Clin Chim Acta 2026;579 (DOI 10.1016/j.cca.2025.120638); no evidence of veterinary third-party reagent availability

checks.claim: In 301 dogs, DGGR-lipase correlated with Spec cPL (rs 0.91); kappa 0.87 and 0.92 at cPL >200 and >=400 ug/L using DGGR cutoffs 143 and 205 U/L; AUC for acute pancreatitis DGGR 0.75 vs cPL 0.76 (Vet Sci 2022).
checks.reason: All figures confirmed (Wolfer, Howard and Peters, Vet Sci 2022). The AUCs for predicting cPL were 0.97 (>200) and 0.99 (>=400). Cutoff 143 U/L gave Se 91.7%, Sp 95.3%; 205 U/L gave Se 97.5%, Sp 96.4%. Both tests had only modest accuracy for a clinical diagnosis of pancreatitis (AUC 0.75 and 0.76). A small 2021 Veterinary Record comparison reported poor DGGR sensitivity, so results vary between studies.

checks.claim: A Bayesian evaluation in Ethiopian cattle found i-ELISA performed best (sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 96.3%), ahead of RBPT and CFT.
checks.reason: The study tested 278 sera from five dairy herds. i-ELISA: Se 96.8% (95% PI 92.3-99.1), Sp 96.3% (91.7-98.8). CFT: Se 94%, Sp 88.5%. RBT: Se 89.6%, Sp 84.5%. These are non-Indian data. A Cote d'Ivoire Bayesian study found a much lower RBT sensitivity (54.9%).

checks.claim: On a Sysmex F-800, canine and feline RBC count and Hgb were stable for 72 h at both 4 C and 25 C. MCV rose by 12 h at 25 C and by 24 h refrigerated. Platelet counts fell significantly by 6 h at 4 C (Vet Clin Pathol 1997).
checks.reason: Confirmed (Pastor et al., Vet Clin Pathol 1997;26(3):138-147), with one limit: the MCV and platelet findings are for dogs only. In cats, WBC counts trended down by 12 h at both temperatures. Feline platelets could not be counted accurately because RBC and platelet populations overlapped, which is worth noting for Mindray feline platelet validation. The analyser is about 30 years old.

checks.claim: IVRI's diagnostics rate card lists PCR for canine parvovirus/CDV/ICH/corona at Rs 600 (ICAR institutions) and Rs 900 (other organizations), and ELISA at Rs 300/400.
checks.reason: Confirmed. The rates are stated as effective from June 2024, and 18% GST is added on top. Feline panleukopenia PCR is also Rs 600/900. The results did not show whether the rates have changed since June 2024.

checks.claim: The VetMAX MastiType kits (bovine mastitis multiplex qPCR) run on the Applied Biosystems 7500/7500 Fast or the QuantStudio 5 Real-Time PCR System.
checks.reason: Thermo Fisher catalog pages for the MastiType Multi Kit (A39227) and Combo Kit (A40290) list exactly these two instruments. The kit covers 15 mastitis pathogens plus a penicillin-resistance gene in four reactions. Fix the citation: the URL the researcher gave (MPBO50) is the VetMAX M. bovis kit page, not the MastiType page. Software requirements are in a separate VeriVet guideline that the search did not return.

checks.claim: In 719 dog samples from Punjab, multiplex PCR found more infections than microscopy: B. gibsoni 8.9%, B. vogeli 1.1%, E. canis 2.6%, H. canis 5.1%.
checks.reason: PCR figures confirmed. The microscopy figures were B. gibsoni 5.0%, B. vogeli 0.1%, E. canis 1.4% and H. canis 1.0%. Agreement between the methods ranged from fair to substantial. A separate Punjab duplex real-time PCR study of 338 dogs (PMC8886702) found 54.1% overall: H. canis 25.4%, B. gibsoni 16.3%, E. canis 10.7%, B. vogeli 1.8%. Prevalence clearly depends on the method and the study.
